First Day of Kindergarten

Your child's first day of kindergarten as their own story: saying goodbye, snack time, new friends — and learning that Mum and Dad always come back.

A personalized picture book in which your child is the hero — and masters this challenge themselves. The first story is free.

Create This Story

The snack box has been picked out and the slippers have their place in the bag — and the closer the big day comes, the more often the question arrives: “Will you stay with me?” For many families, the first day of kindergarten is the first real separation: for the first time, your child puts their hand into that of someone they barely know, while you stand outside the door hoping the tears dry quickly. And quite often, they are not only the child's tears.

At around four, a separation like this is developmentally a big step. Concepts of time such as “until lunchtime” are still abstract at that age — your child simply cannot gauge how long you will be gone. Add a new caregiver, a group full of unfamiliar children and a room full of unknown rules. Separation pain is therefore not a sign that something is wrong; it is the healthy reaction of a securely attached child, and it usually fades within minutes of the goodbye.

This is exactly where stories come in. Seen from the outside, a kindergarten morning suddenly becomes manageable: your child watches the character hang their jacket on their own hook, without having to endure the situation while thinking about it. When that character is your own child, the feeling of “I can do that too” grows with every page. And because the story walks through the whole sequence — goodbye, snack time in the circle, playing, pick-up — your child already knows on the real first day what comes next. The most important message of all: someone always comes back for you.

The personalized kindergarten story shows your child with their own face in precisely these moments: waving at the door, joining a game for the first time, eating their snack next to a new friend — and beaming at pick-up time. The plot takes the uncertainty seriously, lets it exist, and shows in small, familiar steps how a strange place becomes a trusted one. If you would like to try it first: the first story is free.

Read the story several times in the weeks before the start, and borrow a fixed farewell ritual from it — a kiss, a wave at the window, always the same. Say goodbye briefly and clearly; sneaking away undermines trust, even if it feels easier in the moment. Let your child retell the story to the grandparents, which anchors the sequence. And if after six to eight weeks drop-off still ends in big tears every day, talk to the teacher or a parental counselling service — the book accompanies, but does not replace a professional assessment.

What your child learns

Coping with separation, building trust, making new friends, understanding routines, confidence in a group

Recommended age

3-5 years

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I prepare my child for the first day of kindergarten?

If your municipality offers visiting mornings, use them so the room and the teacher are already familiar. Practise the practical things at home: putting on slippers, hanging up the jacket, opening the snack box alone. And in calm moments, describe how a kindergarten morning unfolds — from drop-off to pick-up.

What do I do if my child cries at drop-off?

Stay calm, say goodbye with the same short ritual every time, and then actually leave. The vast majority of children settle within minutes — ask the teacher, she sees it every August. A drawn-out goodbye makes it harder for both of you, not easier.

Should I sneak away while my child is distracted playing?

No — tempting as it is. If your child notices you have vanished, they learn they must keep an eye on you at all times, and the separation anxiety grows. A short, clear goodbye with tears is better in the long run than disappearing unnoticed.

How long does settling into kindergarten take?

It varies a lot — for some children it is days, for others several weeks. Setbacks after weekends, holidays or illness are normal and no cause for alarm. Only if drop-off still ends in real distress every day after six to eight weeks is it worth sitting down with the teacher.

Does a book really help with separation anxiety?

A book won't magic the fear away, but it gives it words and a frame: your child can play through the separation in safety and sees that pick-up always comes. Many children find a story in which they themselves play the lead especially comforting. For pronounced, persistent separation anxiety, however, a book is no substitute for professional advice.
